title: Critical Software is rebuilding itself around AI (200 ppl being layed off)
content:
Critical Software, the Coimbra-based technology company, is being refounded because of AI. "We are refounding the company. There is a before and after artificial intelligence," co-founder and chairman Gonçalo Quadros told the Lusa news agency on Tuesday, according to Público.
Asked about a recent wave of layoffs, Quadros declined to give details but acknowledged that "some people" had been let go because of the changes AI has brought to the company. He did not say how many. The aim, he said, was to keep the organisation agile and fast by cutting whatever makes it less flexible. He added that the company is not currently in a job-cutting process.
Quadros described a sequence inside the company. Routine work went to AI first, notably testing a system and checking how it behaves, which the machine does with what he called "absolutely brutal" effectiveness and efficiency. AI then moved into producing code itself. Two or three years ago that was not the case, he said, but today the machine writes code of "brutal" quality.
Critical Software still develops software today. Quadros believes that, in a not very distant future, most software "will be made by the machine", and says what the company does can no longer be what it has been until now. The company told Público by email that the future of its software development will depend on adapting to the needs of its sectors.
The work that stays is technology for critical systems in aviation, aerospace and automotive. A system that controls an aircraft or ensures a train does not pass a red signal is a piece of technology that includes software but must be designed, verified and validated by humans, Quadros said, and he does not expect that to disappear.
He floated a ten-fold gain: AI might multiply the company's productive capacity by ten, so it could build technology ten times faster. That could make viable systems that were not economically efficient before, because they needed large amounts of software development that a machine can now take on.
Quadros also voiced concern about the race among the big AI developers. If machines reached recursive self-improvement, meaning a system able to optimise itself, and control were lost, he said, "we may be on the edge of the abyss". The probability of something dystopian is higher than it has ever been, he said, without saying whether it is large or small.

report.summary: Critical Software is refounding itself around AI after layoffs, shifting routine testing and coding to machines while keeping human-led critical-systems engineering.
report.background: Critical Software, based in Coimbra, Portugal, has long built software for critical systems in aviation, aerospace, automotive and other safety-sensitive sectors. Its chairman says AI has created a clear before-and-after moment: routine testing and code generation are increasingly handled by machines, changing how software companies organise teams and price work. The article acknowledges layoffs but does not confirm the '200 people' figure in the headline; management declined to give numbers. The restructuring reflects a broader industry shift as AI coding tools improve rapidly, forcing engineering services firms to rethink which tasks need human judgment, verification and domain expertise.
key_points: Critical Software is being 'refounded' around AI, with co-founder Gonçalo Quadros saying there is a before and after artificial intelligence. The company acknowledged some layoffs but did not confirm how many people were affected, despite the headline's 200 figure.

Routine work such as testing systems and checking behaviour moved to AI first. Quadros described the machine's effectiveness as 'absolutely brutal', and said AI now also writes code at a quality that was not possible two or three years ago.

The work that remains is critical-systems technology for aviation, aerospace and automotive. Systems controlling aircraft or rail signals still need human design, verification and validation, and Quadros does not expect that human role to disappear.

Quadros floated a ten-fold productivity gain: AI could let the company build technology ten times faster and make previously uneconomic systems viable. He also warned that recursive self-improvement in AI, if control were lost, could put humanity 'on the edge of the abyss'.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a signal that AI coding is moving from assistant to organisational redesign: firms are not just adding tools but changing team structures, hiring and service models. For developers, routine coding and testing roles face pressure, while skills in verification, safety assurance, systems engineering and domain regulation become more valuable. For regular users, faster and cheaper software development could bring more capable products, but safety-critical systems demand clear accountability and human oversight. The case also highlights a tension: companies are betting on AI productivity while their leaders warn about uncontrolled AI risk.
report.tools: To follow this shift, watch AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot and Cursor, open-source options like Continue and Aider, and coding agents such as OpenHands. For critical systems, explore verification and testing tools including TLA+, CBMC, Kani and SPARK Ada. These show where AI code generation meets formal assurance and human review.
